About

Background and Research Identity

I develop AI methods that learn from heterogeneous urban data, mobility traces, geospatial imagery, and domain-specific text, to model how cities move, change, and grow. I graduated from the Department of Urban and Regional Planning at BUET, where my research evolved across GeoAI, transportation analytics, NLP, and deep learning for geospatial data.

A central theme of my work is the interaction between human mobility and geographic space. Mobility patterns are shaped by land use, accessibility, urban form, and human activity, while geospatial observations reveal how these environments evolve. I am interested in developing AI methods that connect these dimensions to model mobility, spatial dynamics, and changing urban systems, particularly under sparse, heterogeneous, and multi-source data conditions.

My research has included domain-adapted language models for transit-oriented development, travel behavior and metro access-mode analysis, generative learning for cross-sensor geospatial data, and deep learning with satellite imagery. Across these projects, I have become particularly interested in representation learning, generative AI, spatiotemporal modeling, and domain-aware AI, both for discovering patterns in complex spatial data and for forecasting change.

Beyond academic research, I co-founded SpatioTech, a pre-seed venture supported by the ICT Division of Bangladesh and the World Bank, where I work on applied AI and spatial technology for urban problems. This experience has reinforced my interest in connecting methodological research with deployable, data-driven systems for rapidly changing cities, particularly in the Global South.

Going forward, I aim to develop AI models that jointly reason over mobility, space, and heterogeneous urban data, bridging advances in GeoAI and Transportation AI to understand, forecast, and support decisions in complex urban systems.

Transportation Research Part D · Q1 · 2026 Mode Choice · ITS Third Author
Access Mode Choice in Low-Income Megacity: Perceived Walkability and Station Context Effects
Transportation Research Part D, Transport and Environment (Q1)  ·  DOI: 10.1016/j.trd.2026.105421  ·  Third Author
Investigated MRT access mode choice behavior across three station types on MRT Line 6, Dhaka, CBD (Agargaon), residential (Pallabi), and terminal+peripheral (Uttara North). Used a Hybrid Choice Model integrating objective variables with latent perceptions of walkability. Survey of 338 MRT users across three stations using stratified random sampling and face-to-face interviews during morning peak periods. Key findings: rickshaws dominate access (41%), followed by buses (20%) and walking. A distance-based hierarchy governs mode choice, walking for short trips, rickshaws for medium, buses for longer distances. Walkway quality significantly influences access mode choice; street vibrancy and safety show limited effects. Travel time, cost, access time to bus, and station location type are significant determinants. Walking is preferred at residential stations; rickshaws and buses dominate at terminal+peripheral stations.
338 respondents 3 station types Hybrid Choice Model Dhaka MRT Line 6

A Study on Delineation of Core Rural Road Network with Influencing Factors by EWM-TOPSIS Method and Land Use Conversion Pattern in Selected Northern Upazilas in Bangladesh
Arnob Roy, Nabil Fahad, Shuvo Chowhan et al. · Supervised by Md. Musleh Uddin Hasan · International Conference on Urban and Regional Planning, 2025
Field study across 14 upazilas in northern Bangladesh combining two analyses. For core road network: KII and RRA at union level identified 7 influencing factors; Entropy Weighted Method assigned objective weights (growth center connectivity 27.4%, service facility 23.6%, agricultural transport 16%); TOPSIS ranked Village-A roads with 77%–94% match to preliminary networks across all upazilas. For land use conversion: regression model (R²=0.54, p<0.0001) identified change in occupation (r=0.852), population growth (r=0.787), and road proximity (r=0.775) as dominant drivers; agricultural-to-residential conversion was highest at 30.61%; migration significantly associated with conversion pattern (Chi-square=33.712, p=0.039).

Academic Projects

Coursework and studio projects from BUET, Urban Planning, GIS, and Design

Access Mode Choice, Pallabi MRT Station, Dhaka

In-person intercept surveys conducted around Pallabi MRT station catchment. PCA applied to identify key determinants of access mode choice among Bus, Rickshaw, and Walking. Found travel time to station is the dominant factor for working commuters; economic status and trip distance drive modal shifts. Revealed significant differences in access behaviour across income groups within the service coverage zone.

Core Rural Road Network Delineation and Land Use Conversion, 14 Upazilas, Northern Bangladesh

Conference paper presented at the International Conference on Urban and Regional Planning, 2025. First Author. Study covered 14 upazilas across northern Bangladesh (Dhaka, Rangpur, Mymensingh, Rajshahi divisions). Two-part analysis: core rural road network delineation and land use conversion pattern prediction. Read more →

Core Road Network: KII and RRA conducted at union level across 14 upazilas. Seven influencing factors identified (commercial traffic, growth center connectivity, service facility access, transport hub connection, RHD road connectivity, union HQ access, agricultural goods transport). Entropy Weighted Method (EWM) applied for objective factor weighting, growth center connectivity ranked highest (27.4%), followed by service facility (23.6%) and agricultural transport (16%). TOPSIS then ranked Village-A roads upazila-wise. Case study in Sarishabari Upazila: 21 top-ranked roads selected; 77.7% match with preliminary network. Across all 14 upazilas, analytical match rate ranged 77%–94%. Core network achieved ~90% connectivity to growth centers, community clinics and service facilities. Missing link analysis revealed core network connection (35%) and hat/bazaar access (25%) as top community priorities.

Land Use Conversion: Agricultural-to-residential conversion was highest at 30.61%, followed by commercial farming (15.31%) and commercial use (13.27%). Hypothesis testing across 9 variables: Change in Occupation (r=0.852), Population Growth (r=0.787), Location Near Roads (r=0.775) showed strongest positive association. Government intervention had negative correlation (r=−0.647). Migration significantly associated with land conversion (Chi-square=33.712, p=0.039). Linear regression model (R²=0.54, F=12.57, p<0.0001) produced predictive equation incorporating previous land use, population growth, migration, road proximity, occupation change, market need, and government initiative.

Tools: GIS mapping (LGED road network data), R (regression, correlation), KII/RRA field survey, EWM-TOPSIS MCDM. Show less ↑

Regional Plan for Landslide Management, Chittagong Hill Tracts

Procedural regional plan for landslide disaster risk reduction across Rangamati, Khagrachhari, and Bandarban districts, aligned with the Sendai Framework and Bangladesh Disaster Management Act 2012. Key outputs: hazard-based land use zoning, community relocation protocols, nature-based mitigation (reforestation, bioengineering), and a multi-level governance structure integrating Hill District Councils and indigenous community leaders. Addressed critical planning gaps including the absence of demarcated landslide zones and non-enforcement of penalties for illegal hill cutting.

Land Cover Digitization, Daudkandi, Bangladesh

Produced a detailed land cover map of Daudkandi area using ArcGIS Pro through manual digitization. Classified 11 land cover categories across road infrastructure (local, collector, secondary, primary), building typology (tin-shaded, single-storied, multi-storied), open space types (barren, playground, private), waterbodies (pond, seasonal), agricultural lands (permanent and seasonal cropland), and tree canopy. Final output as a publication-quality cartographic map.

ArcGIS ProManual DigitizationLand CoverCartography
Earthquake Vulnerability Assessment, Old Dhaka (Ward Level)

Ward-specific earthquake vulnerability assessment in Old Dhaka using Focus Group Discussions, Key Performance Indicators, and Participatory Rural Appraisal tools. Key findings: widespread resident misconceptions about structural safety; roads critically narrow for emergency access; buildings lack mandatory setbacks due to ancestral plot subdivision patterns; no formal building rules followed. Documented the link between family inheritance structures and structural non-compliance as a systemic planning failure.

Annaya Residential Area Design

Site plan and layout design for a real residential development site following Bangladesh National Building Code (BNBC) 2020 standards. Produced in AutoCAD.
